questions.q: Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers $200$ and $212$ respectively, shows spontaneous $\alpha$-decay with same $Q$ value of $1$ MeV. The ratio of energies of $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is ________.
questions.solution:
In an $\alpha$-decay, the kinetic energy of the emitted $\alpha$-particle is given by the conservation of momentum and energy as:

$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{A - 4}{A} Q$

where $A$ is the mass number of the parent nucleus.

For substance A ($A = 200$):

$K_{\alpha, A} = \dfrac{200 - 4}{200} Q = \dfrac{196}{200} Q$

For substance B ($A = 212$):

$K_{\alpha, B} = \dfrac{212 - 4}{212} Q = \dfrac{208}{212} Q$

The ratio of the energies of the $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is:

$\dfrac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{196}{200} Q}{\dfrac{208}{212} Q} = \dfrac{196}{200} \times \dfrac{212}{208}$

Simplifying the fractions:

$\dfrac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \dfrac{49}{50} \times \dfrac{53}{52} = \dfrac{2597}{2600}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2597}{2600}$

questions.q: The energy released if hydrogen atoms are combined to form $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ is __________ MeV. (Take binding energies per nucleon of $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ as $1.1$ MeV and $7.2$ MeV, respectively)
questions.solution:
The fusion reaction is given by:

$2 ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

Binding energy of one $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ nucleus = $2 \times 1.1 = 2.2$ MeV

Total initial binding energy = $2 \times 2.2 = 4.4$ MeV

Binding energy of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ nucleus = $4 \times 7.2 = 28.8$ MeV

Energy released $\Delta E$ = Final binding energy - Initial binding energy

$\Delta E = 28.8 - 4.4 = 24.4$ MeV

Answer: $24.4$

questions.q: The energy released when $\dfrac{7}{17.13}$ kg of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ is converted into $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ by proton bombardment is $\alpha \times 10^{32}$ eV. The value of $\alpha$ is _______. (Nearest integer) (Mass of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li} = 7.0183$ u, mass of $^{4}_{2}\text{He} = 4.004$ u, mass of proton $= 1.008$ u and $1$ u $= 931$ MeV/c$^2$ and Avogadro number $= 6.0 \times 10^{23}$)
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction for the proton bombardment of Lithium is:

$^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow 2 ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$

The mass defect ($\Delta m$) for the reaction is:

$\Delta m = m(^{7}_{3}\text{Li}) + m(^{1}_{1}\text{H}) - 2m(^{4}_{2}\text{He})$

$\Delta m = 7.0183 + 1.008 - 2(4.004)$

$\Delta m = 8.0263 - 8.008 = 0.0183 \text{ u}$

Energy released per reaction ($Q$) is:

$Q = \Delta m \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 0.0183 \times 931 \text{ MeV} = 17.0373 \text{ MeV}$

Number of moles of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ in $\dfrac{7}{17.13} \text{ kg}$:

$n = \dfrac{\dfrac{7}{17.13} \times 10^3 \text{ g}}{7 \text{ g/mol}} = \dfrac{1000}{17.13} \text{ mol}$

Number of atoms of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$:

$N = n \times N_A = \dfrac{1000}{17.13} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = \dfrac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}$

Total energy released ($E$) is:

$E = N \times Q = \left(\dfrac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}\right) \times (17.0373 \times 10^6 \text{ eV})$

$E = \dfrac{102.2238}{17.13} \times 10^{32} \text{ eV} \approx 5.967 \times 10^{32} \text{ eV}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $\alpha = 6$.

Answer: $6$

questions.q:
Assuming the experimental mass of ${}^{12}_{6}C$ as $12\text{ u}$, the mass defect of ${}^{12}_{6}C$ atom is _______ $\text{MeV}/c^2$.
(Mass of proton $= 1.00727\text{ u}$, mass of neutron $= 1.00866\text{ u}$, $1\text{ u} = 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2$ and $c$ is the speed of the light in vacuum).
questions.solution:
The mass of $6$ protons is $6 \times 1.00727\text{ u} = 6.04362\text{ u}$.

The mass of $6$ neutrons is $6 \times 1.00866\text{ u} = 6.05196\text{ u}$.

Total mass of the constituent nucleons is $6.04362\text{ u} + 6.05196\text{ u} = 12.09558\text{ u}$.

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is the difference between the total mass of the nucleons and the experimental mass of the atom (ignoring electron mass as per the given data):

$\Delta m = 12.09558\text{ u} - 12\text{ u} = 0.09558\text{ u}$

Converting the mass defect into $\text{MeV}/c^2$:

$\Delta m = 0.09558 \times 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2 = 89.03277\text{ MeV}/c^2 \approx 89.03\text{ MeV}/c^2$

Answer: $89.03$

questions.q: Two nuclei of mass number $3$ combine with another nucleus of mass number $4$ to yield a nucleus of mass number $10$. If the binding energy per nucleon for the mass numbers $3$, $4$ and $10$ are $5.6$ MeV, $7.4$ MeV and $6.1$ MeV, respectively, then in the process, $\Delta Mc^2 = $ _____ MeV.
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction is given by:

$2 X^{3} + Y^{4} \rightarrow Z^{10}$

The total binding energy of the reactants is the sum of the binding energies of the two nuclei of mass number $3$ and the nucleus of mass number $4$.

Binding energy of reactants $= 2 \times (3 \times 5.6) + (4 \times 7.4)$

$= 33.6 + 29.6 = 63.2$ MeV

The total binding energy of the product nucleus of mass number $10$ is:

Binding energy of product $= 10 \times 6.1 = 61.0$ MeV

The change in mass energy $\Delta M c^2$ is equal to the difference in the total binding energies of the reactants and the product.

$\Delta M c^2 = |63.2 - 61.0| = 2.2$ MeV

Answer: $2.2$

questions.q: A nucleus has mass number $\alpha$ and radius $R_{\alpha}$. Another nucleus has mass number $\beta$ and radius $R_{\beta}$. If $\beta=8 \alpha$ then $R_{\alpha} / R_{\beta}$ is:
questions.solution:
Nuclear radius follows $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ where $A$ is mass number.
Given $\beta = 8\alpha$, we have $R_\alpha = R_0 \alpha^{1/3}$ and $R_\beta = R_0 (8\alpha)^{1/3} = R_0 \cdot 2 \alpha^{1/3} = 2R_\alpha$.
Thus $R_\alpha/R_\beta = 1/2 = 0.5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: For all elements, greater the mass of the nucleus, greater is the binding energy per nucleon.
Statement II: For all elements, nuclei with less binding energy per nucleon transforms to nuclei with greater binding energy per nucleon.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Statement I is false because binding energy per nucleon does not increase monotonically with mass number. It peaks at Iron-56 and decreases for heavier elements.
Statement II is true. It describes the fundamental principle of nuclear reactions: fission of heavy nuclei (low BE/A) and fusion of light nuclei (low BE/A) both produce nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy in the process. Both processes are energetically favorable for the same reason: moving toward higher stability (higher BE/A).

questions.q: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?
questions.solution:
Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have the same number of nucleons (mass number $A$), but different atomic numbers ($Z$).
In the given options:
(1) $_1^3\text{H}$ and $_2^3\text{He}$: Both have the same mass number $A = 3$. Since they have different atomic numbers ($Z=1$ and $Z=2$), they are isobars.
(2) $_1^2\text{H}$ and $_1^3\text{H}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z=1$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
(3) $_{80}^{198}\text{Hg}$ and $_{79}^{197}\text{Au}$: These have different mass numbers ($198$ and $197$).
(4) $_{92}^{236}\text{U}$ and $_{92}^{238}\text{U}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z=92$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
Thus, the pair $_1^3\text{H}$ and $_2^3\text{He}$ are isobars.

questions.q:
The average energy released per fission for the nucleus of ${ }_{92}^{235} \mathrm{U}$ is 190 MeV. When all the atoms of 47 g pure ${ }_{92}^{235} \mathrm{U}$ undergo fission process, the energy released is $\alpha \times 10^{23} \mathrm{MeV}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
(Avogadro Number $=6 \times 10^{23}$ per mole)
questions.solution:
The number of $^{235}\text{U}$ atoms in 47 g is determined using Avogadro's number.
Molar mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ is 235 g/mol, so the number of moles is $n = 47/235$ mol.
The total number of atoms is $N = (47/235) \times 6 \times 10^{23}$.
Since each fission releases 190 MeV, the total energy released is:
$E_{total} = N \times 190 = \frac{47 \times 6 \times 10^{23}}{235} \times 190 = \frac{47 \times 6 \times 190}{235} \times 10^{23}$ MeV.
Calculating the numerator: $47 \times 6 \times 190 = 282 \times 190 = 53580$.
Therefore: $E_{total} = \frac{53580}{235} \times 10^{23} = 228 \times 10^{23}$ MeV, giving $\alpha = 228$.

questions.q: $7.9 \mathrm{MeV} \alpha$-particle scatters from a target material of atomic number 79. From the given data the estimated diameter of nuclei of the target material is (approximately) $\_\_\_\_$ m. $\left[\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\mathrm{o}}}=9 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{Nm}^{2} / \mathrm{C}^{2}\right.$ and electron charge $\left.=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right]$
questions.solution:
For Rutherford scattering, at the closest approach all kinetic energy converts to electrostatic potential energy.
For alpha particle-nucleus collision:
$K.E. = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Z_1 Z_2 e^2}{r_{min}}$
Where: $Z_1 = 2$ (alpha), $Z_2 = 79$ (gold), $K.E. = 7.9$ MeV
$r_{min} = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{7.9 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$
$r_{min} = 2.88 \times 10^{-14}$ m
The estimated nuclear diameter is approximately:
$d = 2 \times r_{min} = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}$ m

questions.q: For a nucleus of mass number $A$ and radius $R$, the mass density of nucleus can be represented as
questions.solution:
The mass density ( $\rho$) of a nucleus is defined as the ratio of its mass to its volume:
$\rho=$ Mass of nucleus / Volume of nucleus
For a spherical nucleus with radius R , the volume is:
$\text{ Volume }=(4 / 3) \pi R^3$
The mass of the nucleus is related to the mass number A :
$\text{ Mass }-\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \text{ _u }$
(where m_u is the atomic mass unit, approximately $1.66 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$)
Therefore:
$\rho=\left(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u}\right) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{R}^3\right]$
Now, there's an important relationship between the mass number A and nuclear radius R. Empirically, it has been found that:
$\mathrm{R}=\mathrm{Ro} * \mathrm{~A}^{\wedge}(1 / 3)$
Where Ro is a constant approximately equal to $1.2 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}(1.2$ fermi).
Substituting this into the density equation:
$\begin{aligned}
& \rho=\left(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u}\right) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi\left(\mathrm{Ro} \times \mathrm{A}^{\wedge}(1 / 3)\right)^3\right] \\ & \rho=(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{m} \text{ _u }) /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{Ro}^3 \times \mathrm{A}\right] \\ & \rho=\mathrm{m} \_\mathrm{u} /\left[(4 / 3) \pi \mathrm{Ro}^3\right]
\end{aligned}$
This shows that the nuclear density is approximately constant for all nuclei, regardless of their mass number. This is a fundamental property of nuclear matter known as nuclear saturation density.
The numerical value is:
$\rho=2.3 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$

From the statements given below :

(A) The angular momentum of an electron in ${n}^{th}$ orbit is an integral multiple of $h$.

(B) Nuclear forces do not obey inverse square law.

(C) Nuclear forces are spin dependent.

(D) Nuclear forces are central and charge independent.

(E) Stability of nucleus is inversely proportional to the value of packing fraction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
(A) Electron revolves around nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$.

(B) Nuclear force does not follow the inverse square law.

(C) Nuclear forces are spin dependent but charge independent.

(D) Nuclear force is attractive in nature. It is a non central force, meaning it does not depend upon the distance between the particles but rather upon their orientation. Nuclear force is stronger if the spin is parallel; and weak if it is anti parallel.

(E) The negative value (less quantity) of packing fraction indicates that the isotope is stable. Positive value of packing fraction implies unstable (radioactive) nucleus. Also, the stability of the nucleus is inversely proportional to the value of the packing fraction.

questions.solution:
Let the reaction be, $( P ) \to ( X ) + ( Y ) + ( Z )$

Let mass of each daughter nuclei be $m$, then mass defect can be written as $∆ M = M - 3m$.

Now the energy released will be in the form of kinetic energy of the daughter nuclei. Therefore,

questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the number of half lives covered by the radioactive material is given by

$n = \dfrac{t}{{T}_{\dfrac{1}{2}}} . . . \left(1\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) to calculate the number of half lives covered.

$\begin{cases}n & = & \dfrac{15years}{5years} \\ & = & 3\end{cases}$

The relation between the amount of radioactive substance after certain time can be written as

$N = {N}_{0}{2}^{- n} . . . \left(2\right)$

Substitute the value of $n$ into equation (2) to obtain the fraction of the remaining substance.

$\begin{cases}N & = & {N}_{0}{2}^{- 3} \\ & ⇒ & \dfrac{N}{{N}_{0}} = \dfrac{1}{8}\end{cases}$

Hence, the amount of the decayed substance can be written as

$\begin{cases}1 - \dfrac{N}{{N}_{0}} & = & 1 - \dfrac{1}{8} \\ & = & \dfrac{7}{8}\end{cases}$

questions.q: A nucleus with mass number $242$ and binding energy per nucleon as $7 . 6MeV$ breaks into two fragment each with mass number $121$. If each fragment nucleus has binding energy per nucleon as $8 . 1MeV,$ the total gain in binding energy is $_______MeV$.
questions.solution:
Binding energy is given by $E = ∆ m{c}^{2}$

where $∆ m$ is the mass defect.

The energy per nucleon of the nucleus having mass number $242$ is $7 . 6MeV$.

The initial binding energy is,

$BE = 242 \times 7 . 6MeV$

The energy per nucleon of the nucleus with mass number $121$ is $8 . 1MeV$.

Therefore, binding energy is

$BE ' = 2\left(121 \times 8 . 1MeV\right)$

The gain in the binding energy is

$BE ' - BE = ( 8 . 1 – 7 . 6 ) \times 242MeV = 121MeV$

$= 121MeV$

Decay law for both process can be written as,

$\dfrac{d{N}_{1}}{dt} = - {\lambda}_{1}N . . . Eq ( 1 )$ and

$\dfrac{d{N}_{2}}{dt} = - {\lambda}_{2}N . . . Eq ( 2 )$

Hence, net decay will become

$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \dfrac{d{N}_{1}}{dt} + \dfrac{d{N}_{2}}{dt} = - ( {\lambda}_{1} + {\lambda}_{2} ) N$

$⇒ \dfrac{ln2}{{t}_{\dfrac{1}{2}}} = \dfrac{ln2}{300} + \dfrac{ln2}{30}$

$⇒ t\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{300}{11}$

Hence, required value of $\alpha = 300$.

When a radioactive nucleus emits $1\alpha$-particle, its mass number decreases by $4$ and the atomic number decreases by $2$. $⇒ P = 92 - 5$

$⇒ P = 87$.

questions.q:
Following statements related to radioactivity are given below :
(A) Radioactivity is a random and spontaneous process and is dependent on physical and chemical conditions.
(B) The number of undecayed nuclei in the radioactive sample decays exponentially with time.
(C) Slope of the graph of ${\log}_{e}$ (no. of undecayed nuclei) vs. time represents the reciprocal of mean life time $\left(τ\right)$.
(D) Product of decay constant $\left(\lambda\right)$ and half-life time $\left(T\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is not constant.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Radioactive decay is a random and spontaneous process, it depends on unbalancing of nucleus. This process is dependent on the law of conservation of charge.

We know that, $N = {N}_{0}{e}^{- \lambdat} . . . \left(1\right), Where, $N$=number of decayed nuclei in the sample at time $t and {N}_{0} =$initial number of nuclei.

Hence, total number of undecayed nuclei ${N}_{0} - N$

Thus, ${N}_{0} - N = {N}_{0}$\left(1 - {e}^{- \lambdat}\right)$

This shows that the total number of undecayed nuclei decays exponentially with time.

Taking log both sides of equation $\left(1\right)$

$lnN = - \lambdat + ln{N}_{0}$

So, slope $= - \lambda$ (reciprocal of mean life time)

Half life time $T\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{ln2}{\lambda}$

Then, $\lambda \times T\dfrac{1}{2} = ln2 = constant$

Hence, (B) and (C) are correct only.

Ratio of number of moles of substance in the beginning will be, $\dfrac{{\left({N}_{0}\right)}_{A}}{{\left({N}_{0}\right)}_{B}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{{10}^{- 2}kg}{{M}_{A}}}{\dfrac{{10}^{- 2}kg}{{M}_{B}}} = \dfrac{{M}_{B}}{{M}_{A}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Number of half-life in $16s$ for element $A$ will be, ${n}_{A} = \dfrac{16}{4} = 4$

Number of half-life in $16s$ for element $B$ will be, ${n}_{B} = \dfrac{16}{8} = 2$

Hence, ratio of number of nuclei after $16s$ will be, $= \dfrac{{\left({N}_{0}\right)}_{A} \times {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{{n}_{A}}}{{\left({N}_{0}\right)}_{B} \times {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{{n}_{B}}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{4 - 2} = \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{25}{100}$

Thus, value of $x$ is $25$.

questions.q: A radioactive nucleus decays by two different processes. The half-life for the first process is $10s$ and that for the second is $100s$. The effective half-life of the nucleus is close to:
questions.solution:
Using the equation of radioactive decay law,

$- \dfrac{dN}{dt} = {\lambda}_{1}N + {\lambda}_{2}N . . . ( 1 )$

$- \dfrac{dN}{dt} = \left({\lambda}_{1} + {\lambda}_{2}\right)N . . . ( 2 )$

Where,

$- \dfrac{d N}{d t}$ is the rate of decay

${\lambda}_{1,}{\lambda}_{2}$ are decay constant for two different processes

$N$ is the number of atoms.

Now applying the decay law for the combine process, we get

$- \dfrac{dN}{dt} = {\lambda}_{eff}N . . . ( 3 )$

Equating equation (1) and (2) we get

${\lambda}_{eff} = \left({\lambda}_{1} + {\lambda}_{2}\right) . . . ( 4 )$

Now the half life of the radioactive nucleus is given by,

$\lambda = \dfrac{ln\left(2\right)}{T} . . . ( 5 )$

Where, $T$ is the half life of the radioactive nucleus

Using equation (5) equation (4) becomes,

$\dfrac{ln\left(2\right)}{T} = \dfrac{ln\left(2\right)}{{T}_{1}} + \dfrac{ln\left(2\right)}{{T}_{2}}$

$\dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{{T}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{T}_{2}}$

$\dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{100} = \dfrac{11}{100}$

$⇒ T = \dfrac{100}{11} \approx 9s$

 $\frac{100-\lambda N}{100}=$ e^{-\lambda t} \\
